newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's orange industry coughs up higher prices.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's orange industry coughs up higher prices.

text.p: Sao Paulo orange growers are being paid up to 40 percent more for new crop oranges this year in what they are interpreting as an industry effort to prevent producers from switching to more profitable crops.
Farmers, who have long been campaigning for an increase in prices, are currently receiving an average of $2.50 per 40.8 kg box of oranges compared with $1.80 at the same time last year.
"There is a lot of preoccupation that production will drop," said Leonardo Kossoy, president of the Association of Citrus Growers of Sao Paulo State (Aciesp).

Although Sao Paulo is forecast to produce a record 405 million boxes in 1996/97, small growers are increasingly diversifying into planting crops with better profit margins, such as tropical fruits, dairy products and sugarcane.
The industry is worried that medium and large producers will follow suit unless they can see a better return on their investment, Kossoy said.
"With the current price of juice, it's a price that the industry can afford," said an analyst who requested anonymity.
"The industry doesn't want to break the producer. It's difficult for the producer to survive two or three years at $1.50 per box," the analyst said.

However, increased competition between domestic processors is also likely contributing to the price hike, which comes at a time when international markets are flaccid, said Michael McDougall, director of commodities futures at Fimat Futures.
"It's hard to believe processors will pay more than they have to just to please the growers," he said.
"Several large producers, such as Cargill and Dreyfus, have expanded production capacity over the last few years and smaller processors have been trying to get in on the act," he said.
"Production capacity has increased to the point where even with increased (orange) production, processors are fighting against each other for fruit to guarantee production (of juice)," he said.
This year's higher prices are mainly being offered for longer-term contracts, Kossoy said.

"This gives producers the option to keep going and basically the industry is (paying higher prices) to medium and large growers," he added. "It's sufficient to harvest the oranges, transport them and maybe cover costs."
